title: Lower abdominal pain that analgesia would not touch

source.citation: Lin PH, Liang CY, Huang PY. Superior mesenteric embolus accompanied by renal infarction associated with atrial fibrillation successfully treated by anticoagulants: A CARE-compliant case report. Medicine (Baltimore). 2025;104(51):e46740.

presentation.chiefComplaint: Lower abdominal pain for three hours
presentation.hpi: Three hours of persistent, dull lower abdominal pain, 5/10 in severity, with mild nausea. No urinary symptoms.

exam: Moderate lower abdominal tenderness without rebound tenderness or guarding
McBurney, Rovsing, psoas and obturator signs negative

imaging.finding: Segmental filling defect in the superior mesenteric artery (SMA); extensive right renal infarction; no imaging evidence of bowel ischemia
Normal ejection fraction and fractional shortening; no intracardiac thrombus or valvular abnormality

diagnosis.primary: Acute superior mesenteric artery embolism (occlusive arterial mesenteric ischemia without bowel infarction) with right renal infarction, cardioembolic from atrial fibrillation

management: Intramuscular analgesia; the pain persisted, prompting contrast-enhanced CT
General surgery consulted: no operation, as there was no imaging evidence of bowel ischemia and no peritonitis
Admitted to cardiology for IV hydration and subcutaneous enoxaparin
After 5 days switched to oral edoxaban 60 mg daily
Transient hematuria one day after starting anticoagulation, settling within 48 h
outcome: Recovered without surgery (appetite and bowel motility returned) and was discharged after one week on edoxaban. Symptom-free despite persistent atrial fibrillation; renal function unchanged at 3 months and no signs of vascular occlusion or bleeding at 7 months.
teachingPoints: Abdominal pain that persists despite analgesia, with few abdominal signs, in an older patient with atrial fibrillation should prompt immediate CT angiography for mesenteric ischemia.
Normal white cell count and CRP do not exclude acute mesenteric ischemia; D-dimer is sensitive but non-specific.
Emboli are often multiple: a renal infarct can cause flank pain and hematuria that mimic ureteric colic.
Start full anticoagulation as soon as the diagnosis is made and involve vascular and general surgery; revascularization is the norm, and laparotomy is needed for peritonitis or bowel necrosis.
Selected patients without bowel ischemia or peritonitis, as here, may recover on anticoagulation alone, but only under close surgical observation.

questions.q: Which investigation is most appropriate now?
questions.extra: Pain unchanged after intramuscular analgesia. WBC 7930/µL, CRP 1.35 mg/L, creatinine 1.10 mg/dL. Urinalysis: blood positive (50 RBC/µL; 5–10 RBC/hpf).
options: Non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder
Ultrasound of the appendix and pelvis
Contrast-enhanced CT angiography of the abdomen
Discharge with analgesia and outpatient colonoscopy
questions.explanation: Pain out of proportion to the examination in an older patient demands exclusion of vascular causes (mesenteric ischemia, renal infarction, aneurysm); the ESVS 2017 mesenteric guideline recommends immediate CT angiography when acute mesenteric ischemia is suspected. A non-contrast stone CT would miss both the arterial occlusion and the renal infarct.

questions.q: What is the most likely mechanism of these findings?
questions.extra: CT: segmental filling defect in the superior mesenteric artery and an extensively infarcted right kidney; no signs of bowel ischemia. ECG: atrial fibrillation. D-dimer 6.08 mg/L.
options: In situ atherothrombosis at the SMA origin
Non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia from low flow
questions.explanation: Occlusions in two arterial beds at once (SMA and right renal artery) in a patient with atrial fibrillation point to cardioembolism; emboli tend to lodge more distally and cause more limited ischemia than atherothrombosis at the SMA origin. Non-occlusive ischemia needs low cardiac output or vasopressors, and venous thrombosis would show an occluded mesenteric vein.

questions.q: What should be started immediately once the diagnosis is confirmed?
questions.extra: No peritonitis; CT shows no bowel ischemia. Hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL, platelets 192,000/µL, INR 0.98.
options: Aspirin alone with observation on a general ward
Systemic IV alteplase at stroke dosing
Therapeutic anticoagulation with heparin and surgical review
questions.explanation: The ESVS 2017 and WSES 2022 guidelines recommend immediate full anticoagulation with heparin for acute arterial mesenteric occlusion, with urgent surgical and vascular assessment for revascularization; laparotomy is for peritonitis or suspected necrosis. Without bowel ischemia or peritonitis, this patient recovered on enoxaparin then edoxaban under close observation.

evidence.quote: A 70-year-old woman presented to our emergency department with persistent lower abdominal dull pain for three hours.
The severity of pain was 5 on a scale of 10.
She complained of mild nausea but denied urinary symptoms.
She had a history of hypertension and dyslipidemia under satisfactory medical control but denied other known systemic diseases.
along with her previous prescriptions of rosuvastatin and propranolol for dyslipidemia and atrial fibrillation, respectively
she was alert (GCS: E4M6V5)
afebrile (body temperature: 36.0ºC) with stable hemodynamics (heart rate: 74 per minute; blood pressure: 131/81 mm Hg)
Her respiration was smooth at a rate of 18 per minute with an arterial oxygen saturation of 99% on room air.
Physical examination revealed moderate lower abdominal tenderness on palpation without rebound tenderness or muscle guarding.
McBurney's sign, Rovsing's sign, psoas sign, and obturator sign were all negative.

evidence.quote: Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count: 7930/mL, hemoglobin concentration: 14.6 g/dL, hematocrit: 44.1%, platelet count: 192000/mL, neutrophil: 71.2%, lymphocyte: 24.5%
alanine transaminase: 30 U/L, plasma creatinine: 1.10 mg/dL, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR): 52, and a C-reactive protein: 1.35 mg/L
international normalized ratio (INR): 0.98, and activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT): 28.5 seconds
Urinalysis demonstrated the presence of occult blood (50 RBCs/microliter) and trace amount of blood on microscopic examination (5–10 RBCs/HPF).
Due to refractory abdominal pain after intramuscular analgesics
a segmental filling defect in the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) … coupled with right renal infarction
Enhanced abdominal computed tomography showing (A) a filling defect inside the superior mesenteric artery (arrow), and (B) an extensively infarcted right kidney (arrowheads).
the D-dimer level was elevated at 6.08 mg/L (normally < 0.55 mg/L)
Electrocardiogram demonstrated atrial fibrillation.
After consultation with a general surgeon, the option of surgery was declined due to the lack of imaging evidence suggestive of bowel ischemia … absence of clinical signs of peritonitis
She was admitted to the cardiology ward for intravenous hydration and anticoagulation with subcutaneous enoxaparin.
Echocardiography showed normal ejection fraction and fractional shortening without evidence of thrombus or valvular anomaly.
After 5 days of enoxaparin treatment, anticoagulant was switched to oral edoxaban at a daily dose of 60 mg
No surgical follow-up was needed because of improvement in appetite and bowel motility.
Despite transient hematuria that occurred one day after the initiation of anticoagulant treatment, the condition subsided within 48 hours after its first appearance.
Because of general improvement, she was discharged to outpatient care 1 week after admission.
She was regularly followed in the cardiology clinic and remained symptom-free despite persistent atrial fibrillation shown on electrocardiogram 1 week after discharge.
Her latest blood biochemical study 3 months after discharge showed renal function (creatinine: 1.15 mg/dL, eGFR: 50) comparable to that during her first visit
No clinical signs suggestive of vascular occlusion or coagulopathy (e.g., bruising, gastrointestinal hemorrhage) were noted at the latest follow-up seven months after discharge.
An enhanced abdominal computed tomographic scan revealed a filling defect in the SMA and an infarcted right kidney suggestive of a diagnosis of SMA embolism.
our patient was considered to experience an embolic condition considering the limited regions of ischemia and the presence of more than one occlusive lesion
